claims.text: High configurational entropy promotes preferential surface segregation of oxidation-prone elements such as Al or Cr during high-temperature oxidation.
Preferential surface segregation of Al or Cr leads to rapid formation of a continuous protective oxide layer.
The oxide layer formed by the segregated oxidation-prone elements is retained and remains adherent.
The continuous protective oxide layer significantly slows further oxidation relative to conventional alloys.
The proposed initial material is a homogenized, single-phase high-entropy alloy containing multiple near-equimolar principal elements, including elements with high oxygen affinity.
The proposed initial material has minimal surface segregation before oxidation.
High configurational entropy alters diffusion thermodynamics in the alloy.
The entropy-related change in diffusion thermodynamics enhances migration of selected oxidation-prone elements to the surface.
Surface-enriched oxidation-prone elements rapidly oxidize to form a dense, stable oxide layer.
The dense, stable oxide layer acts as a barrier to further oxygen ingress.
Compared with a conventional alloy having similar oxidation-resistant-element content but lower configurational entropy, the high-entropy alloy will form a more uniform oxide scale.
Compared with the conventional-alloy baseline, the high-entropy alloy will form a more adherent oxide scale.
Compared with the conventional-alloy baseline, the high-entropy alloy will exhibit a lower oxide growth rate.
Compared with the conventional-alloy baseline, the high-entropy alloy will show less oxidation-induced weight gain over time.
The proposed mechanism applies to single-phase high-entropy solid solutions oxidized at approximately 800–1000 °C when diffusion-driven segregation is active.
The mechanism may not apply to multiphase alloys or lower-temperature regimes where diffusion is limited.
The magnitude of improvement in oxide formation and oxidation kinetics depends on alloy composition and test conditions.
